    does not exist when the box initializes, and it comes to exist
    in two ways, each a session acting as `state_owner`: the
    backend's first open, and every restore, whose `--clean` drops

    this commit builds restores only into a box that has the role.

head: 80091e1c5b6ef869577b06bbaa40ef24c31090b2
text:
An alert keyed `kluster-ops/drift-trigger` is the trigger's: no
drift run started that week, and the step that failed in the ops
repo's run says why. *The client id and the key are in place*
names the empty slot: `operator-stack github up` writes the
variable, and `credentials derived sync --only github-trigger-key`
refills the secret. A failed mint is a client id or a key that is
not the trigger App's — a key replaced on the App's page and not yet
recorded and synced (credentials.md §3) — or the App no longer
installed on this repo. A failed dispatch carries GitHub's
refusal: an installation without Actions: write, or a `drift.yml`
on `main` that is disabled or has lost its `workflow_dispatch`
trigger. Once the cause is gone, fire the trigger by hand,
`gh workflow run drift-trigger.yml --repo Aetf/kluster-ops`, and
the drift run it dispatches is that week's.

head: e3a794e4fd410141f9fa6d43a09420f287795ffe
text:
"""The scrape jobs whose series the rules read by name alone, each by the `job` label vmagent gives it.

The operator's scrape of one of its own objects -- a vmsingle, vmagent or
alertmanager -- takes the job from the name of the object's Service
(`servicescrape.go` L209-220 at operator v0.74.0), which is the object's
`PrefixedName`; the stack names its objects `stack_fullname`, and the
history store is the component's. kube-state-metrics' is
`KUBE_STATE_METRICS_JOB`.

What each exports is the namespace its exporter names its families in:
`kube_` for kube-state-metrics, the API server's own `kube_apiserver_`
families apart, and `alertmanager_` and `vmagent_` for those two.
VictoriaMetrics names every one of its components' series `vm_`, so a
`vm_` name is claimed by the components whose source registers it: the
count of rows a limit ignored by the stores' ingestion and by vmagent
(`lib/timeserieslimits`, which `app/vmagent` and `app/vminsert` import
and `app/vmalert` does not, at VictoriaMetrics v1.150.0).

Nothing the program declares holds these claims, since no scrape here
keeps only what it names; the recent store corroborates them. Grouped by
`job`, each claim's series -- `{__name__=~"kube_.+"}` without the API
server's, `alertmanager_.+`, `vmagent_.+` and `vm_rows_ignored_total` --
come from the jobs claiming it and no other (Aetf/kluster-ops#833, on
2026-11-17), and `up` carries each job named here at 1. operations.md
§6.4 gives the queries, which are run again when an exporter changes.
"""

context:
Neither `/tmp` nor the home directory keeps a dead workspace. One whose
work is merged or abandoned is a trap for the next agent, which can
read a stale copy of a file it is about to edit. `jj workspace list` is
the census that shows them, a directory that was deleted without being
forgotten included: that one lists under its recorded path like any
other, with nothing to say the directory is gone, and `jj workspace
forget` clears it. A worktree workspace deleted that way also leaves
git's record of the worktree behind, which `git worktree list` marks
`prunable`, `forget` no longer clears, and `git worktree prune` in the
primary removes.

head: c6ecf91f1c757b7de1e0f91dafb2e04211ab61cd
text:
How code in this repository is organized and written. Distilled from the
2026-08-28 physical-stack review (ops#87); the review gate in AGENTS.md
holds new code to it. Rules here are about *structure and style*;
what the system does is the declarative/ and physical/ docs' topic.

context:
-   **Weekly drift check (2026-08-24)**: a `workflow_dispatch`
    workflow in this repo, `drift.yml`, runs
    `pulumi preview --refresh --expect-no-changes`
    on all four stacks (physical in the ungated `physical-plan`
    environment — the accepted posture above, zero clicks). **Its
    schedule is in the ops repo**, because this repo carries no
    `schedule:` trigger: GitHub disables a public repository's
    scheduled workflow after 60 days without activity (the
    scheduled-census bullet below). There `drift-trigger.yml`, on
    `17 6 * * 1` (Mondays at 06:17 UTC) and by hand, mints an
    installation token of the **trigger App**, `kluster-trigger` — a
    second single-purpose GitHub App, installed on this repo alone and
    carrying **Actions: write only**, so it can start runs and never
    push code — for this repo alone, and dispatches `drift.yml` on
    `main` with it. The App's client id reaches that workflow as the
    ops repo's `TRIGGER_APP_CLIENT_ID` variable, which the `github`
    stack writes from `conventions.forge.TRIGGER_APP`, and its key as
    the ops repo's `TRIGGER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` secret, which
    `credentials derived sync --only github-trigger-key` pushes from
    the escrow (credentials.md §3). Two Apps rather than one because
    GitHub scopes permissions per App (register rows in
    credentials.md). The trigger does not wait for the run it starts
    or read its verdict, which is the drift run's own alert job's to
    report: the trigger's alert says only whether a run was
    dispatched, a `heartbeat` when it was and otherwise an
    `actionable` alert keyed `kluster-ops/drift-trigger` whose
    playbook is §3.2, posted by the alert job every ops-repo workflow
    ends in. A run started by hand here, as
    physical/gateway-cutover.md §8.3 starts one, is the same run with
    a person in place of the trigger. A diff fails the run, and a
    failed run ends in the alert job (the alert-producer bullet
    above): an `actionable` alert keyed `kluster/drift`, whose
    playbook is §3.2. Keyed by the workflow, a drift that persists is
    to be one open issue collecting a comment a week rather than a
    page a week. **As of 2026-09-25, how the human learns of it is
    half built**: the producer posts the alert, and the ops repo's
    dispatch handler that would turn it into a push and an issue does
    not exist, so a diff is a failed workflow run and nothing more.
    `--refresh` is load-bearing for the second source: a plain
    preview diffs code against *cached* state and never queries
    providers, so a console hand-edit leaves code == state and
    reports zero diff — only the device files would surface without it
    (`DeviceFile`, `DeviceDirectory` and `DeviceArtifact` all read the
    device in `diff`, architecture.md §5.2). A preview's refresh
    writes nothing: the refreshed state is compared and discarded, so
    the same diff fails every weekly run until it is reconciled
    (§3.2). This closes the "hand edits never surface" gap that
    deleting the post-merge preview left open. On `physical` the
    preview also takes `--run-program`, and on that stack alone: a
    refresh builds each provider from its inputs in state before the
    program runs, and the libvirt provider reads by path two working
    files that only the program writes, which a fresh runner lacks
    (physical/homelab-host.md §6). Every other stack's providers are
    built from values their inputs in state carry whole.

head: 6df7cb69a6c7b3aaf69a59387841bbed3f3cc31c
text:
**A client that names a raw HTTPS port's server with no port is
answered on 443, by name, with a redirect to that port.** That is a
`Redirect` row beside the `Port`: on each Gateway it sets, the
Gateway ends TLS on the zone's wildcard certificate and answers every
request with a `308` to the same name at the port, path and query kept,
forwarding to nothing and asking no gate. A client certificate is
presented on the raw port's leg alone, where the pod asks for it. It is
how the discovery server keeps the address every device holds,
`https://syncapi.<primary>` with no port
([rfc-008](../rfc/rfc-008-workload-migration.md) §4.1,
[Aetf/kluster-ops#723](https://github.com/Aetf/kluster-ops/issues/723)).
The row stands in for a `Passthrough`, which Cilium cannot serve beside
the zone's wildcard listener, and becomes one when the pinned Cilium can
(the comment on its pin in `Pulumi.yaml`).

head: 6df7cb69a6c7b3aaf69a59387841bbed3f3cc31c
text:
A `Passthrough` row, TLS the pod terminates on 443 by name, is refused:
Cilium drops a passthrough listener together with the zone's wildcard
listener on the same port (§6.7). Such a pod is a raw `Port` instead,
and a client that names it with no port is answered by a `Redirect`
row: on each Gateway it sets, an HTTPRoute on the zone's wildcard
listener whose one rule is a `308` to the same name at that port, with
no backend and no gate. The discovery server is the case
([Aetf/kluster-ops#723](https://github.com/Aetf/kluster-ops/issues/723)).

head: d7e431da7bc0466ff388be5ae2e0cc88a2b4ee70
text:
**A container a case creates keeps its output in a file of its own**: it
carries `--log-driver=k8s-file`, `LOG_TO_FILE` in
`tests/process_sessions.py`, whatever the host's default driver is.
`podman logs` reads back what the log driver kept, and the `journald`
driver keeps only what the journal did not drop. The journal rate-limits
per unit, and every rootless container's `conmon` sits in the user's
`user@<uid>.service`, so all of a run's containers share one budget, and a
full parallel run spends it: a suppressed line never reaches
`podman logs`, and a wait for it ends only at its bound. The same check that refuses an unarmed container refuses
a `podman run` or `podman create` that does not carry that driver, or names
another beside it, so a case cannot leave the option out. A case may read
an application's own log file inside the container instead of
`podman logs`, as `tests/test_apps_jellyfin.py` reads its server's; the
container carries the driver all the same.

head: afe7684a6eb63e6fd5e43f2769893f06d1987e56
text:
The chain starts by a dispatch, since `deploy.yml` takes
`workflow_dispatch`, and no pull request precedes it. A dispatched
run checks out `main`, so `up-k8s-base` and `up-apps` read the
kubeconfig copies `main` holds, and those open the rebuilt cluster
as they open it for the refreshes: step 5 issued the `Kubeconfig`
again under the kept PKI and for the kept endpoint, and a stale copy
keeps opening the cluster while its certificate is valid and its
authority trusted (§2.5), neither of which a rebuild changes. So
the sync of the new copy is housekeeping, and it rides in step 9's
pull request. The chain runs: `plan-physical` finds no diff, and
`up-k8s-base` and `up-apps` are both stacks' first `up` on an empty
cluster, over ciphertexts the new controller cannot open, so
whatever reads one waits for step 9's sitting.

context:
"""What stops a mistake from becoming a bill (nodes.md §3.2).

The tenancy is Pay-As-You-Go, and **there is no hard spending cap**. The
failure mode of a pay-as-you-go tenancy is inverted from a free one — a limits
change or a fat-fingered shape gets *billed* instead of *killed*, which is the
survivable half of the trade but only if something is watching. Two mechanisms
watch, and only one of them can actually refuse anything:

-   **Compartment quotas** are resource-side and enforced at creation time: a
    request for a shape outside the declared envelope fails. This is the real
    guardrail.
-   **A budget with alert rules** is a notification, evaluated roughly daily.
    It cannot stop spending; it reports that spending happened. It exists for
    the costs quotas cannot express — egress, request counts, a price change.

**A1 is bounded twice, per availability domain and per region**, and an
instance is created only where both admit it. Both bounds hold exactly the
fleet, so the cloud refuses a node beyond it whoever asks: a twin launched
beside the node it would replace, which would take a live member out of etcd
(declarative/physical.md §1), a fat-fingered node count, a stray instance. A
node is replaced by terminating it first and creating it again (operations.md
§3.1), so no replacement needs room beside the fleet.

-   **Per AD**, the bound is one node's worth: the fleet is one node per AD
    (nodes.md §5), so a second node in an AD is refused there. Block storage
    is scoped per AD the same way.
-   **Per region**, the bound is the fleet, what `conventions.CLOUD_NODES`,
    `NODE_OCPUS` and `NODE_MEMORY_GB` declare. That is the compartment's
    ceiling: in a region with more ADs than the fleet has nodes, the per-AD
    numbers admit a node in each AD the fleet leaves empty, and the regional
    quota is what refuses it.

The regional bound is looser than the free envelope, and deliberately so: the
fleet itself bills past it (nodes.md §3.2).

**Statement order is load-bearing.** Within one policy, a later statement
supersedes an earlier one for the same quota, so the wildcard `zero` comes
first and the shapes the design actually creates are set after it. The effect
is a default-deny on compute: every shape family is unavailable except the one
the cluster runs on.
"""

context:
"""Run as the pod runs it after the merge over `KEPT`, the server answers the kubelet's probe and each request the Gateways forward.

Each caller asks from an address of its own in the network the server's
container shares: from loopback, or from the pod's own address, the
server exempts a request from its filter. The kubelet probes from the
address `cilium_host` holds, in the pod range, with no forwarded
address. Envoy connects from the pod range and appends its peer to
`X-Forwarded-For`, and the server, which trusts the pod ranges, judges
the request by the address before Envoy's: Cloudflare's edge for the
internet route, the client for one that dials the balancer, and a home
client, on a subnet `KEPT` counts as local, for `media`. `KEPT`'s
allowlist leaves out every address but the home client's, so a server
that kept it would refuse both internet callers. `KEPT` also names
another port, a base path, a bind address the pod does not have and IPv4
off, so a server that read it unmerged would answer none. While it
starts the server answers from a placeholder, which listens whatever the
base path, so the callers ask once the server has logged its start
complete, in the log directory its image names.

The network settings the server logs are read from that same file. The
server logs them while it builds its services, ahead of its start
complete, and writes the file in the order it logs, so they are there
by the time the callers ask. The container's own output is no such
record: podman hands it to its log driver, and a journald driver keeps
what the journal's per-unit rate limit lets through, which every
container of the user shares.
"""
